items.prompt: What's the core difference between responsive design and adaptive design?
choices: Responsive relies mostly on bold, saturated colors; adaptive relies mostly on grayscale and muted tones for its UI
Responsive is one fluid layout that reflows continuously; adaptive is a small set of fixed layouts, each matched to a device class
They're really just two different marketing names that both refer to the exact same single underlying technique
Adaptive design only ever functions correctly on mobile devices; responsive design only ever functions on desktop
items.explanation: Responsive design uses one layout with relative units and breakpoints that continuously reflows as width changes. Adaptive design picks among a small number of discrete, fixed layouts built for known device classes — there's no continuous reflow between them.
items.reference:
🌊 Responsive: one fluid layout
🧩 Adaptive: fixed layout set

Why: responsive reflows continuously from actual width; adaptive matches the closest of a few pre-built templates.

items.prompt: A site ships three completely separate templates — one for phone, one for tablet, one for desktop — and the server picks the closest match for each visitor. Which strategy is this?
choices: Responsive design, since serving three completely separate templates per device is considered standard responsive practice
Adaptive design
Fluid layout, since fluid layout is defined specifically by serving multiple separate fixed templates per visitor
This isn't actually considered a real, recognized layout strategy at all in modern front-end development practice
items.explanation: Picking among a small, fixed set of pre-built templates based on device class — with no continuous reflow between them — is the definition of adaptive design.
items.reference:
🌊 Responsive: one fluid layout
🧩 Adaptive: fixed layout set

Why: responsive reflows continuously from actual width; adaptive matches the closest of a few pre-built templates.

items.prompt: In responsive design, what decides how the layout looks at any given moment?
choices: A designer manually and individually picks which specific layout gets served to each visitor who loads the page
The browser, continuously, based on the actual current viewport width
The device's underlying operating system, which reports a fixed layout preference to the browser ahead of rendering
A single fixed layout that gets chosen exactly once at the moment of page load and is never re-evaluated after that
items.explanation: Responsive layouts use relative units and breakpoints so the browser recomputes the layout continuously as width changes — there's no single moment where 'the layout' gets decided and locked in.
items.reference:
🌊 Responsive: one fluid layout
🧩 Adaptive: fixed layout set

Why: responsive reflows continuously from actual width; adaptive matches the closest of a few pre-built templates.

items.prompt: What is a 'breakpoint' in responsive design?
choices: A bug in the stylesheet that accidentally breaks the overall layout, usually caused by a missing closing bracket
A viewport width where the layout's structure changes, e.g. three columns become two
The absolute maximum width that a page's container is technically allowed to ever grow to, as a hard limit
A specialized tool built into browser developer tools specifically for stepping through and debugging JavaScript code
items.explanation: A breakpoint is a specific viewport width, written as an @media condition, where the arrangement of elements changes — not where every value changes continuously (that's fluid layout).
items.reference:
@media (min-width: 768px) { ... } — rules inside only apply once the viewport reaches that width.

Why: a breakpoint marks where structure changes, not a general 'things get different' point.

items.prompt: A three-column grid stays three columns from 320px all the way up to 3840px, with columns getting painfully narrow on phones. What's missing?
choices: Simply adding more images to the three columns, so each one feels visually fuller even at very narrow widths
A breakpoint that collapses the grid to fewer columns at narrow widths
Simply increasing the overall font size used across the grid, so the narrow columns feel less cramped to read
Nothing at all is missing here — a rigid three-column layout is always the objectively correct choice regardless of width
items.explanation: Without a breakpoint restructuring the grid at narrow widths, the same column count gets forced into every viewport, crushing columns on phones. A breakpoint is exactly the tool for a discrete structural change like column count.
items.reference:
@media (min-width: 768px) { ... } — rules inside only apply once the viewport reaches that width.

Why: a breakpoint marks where structure changes, not a general 'things get different' point.

items.prompt: What does 'fluid layout' add on top of breakpoints?
choices: A dedicated mechanism for smoothly animating transitions between two different pages as a visitor navigates around
Sizes expressed as a formula relative to the viewport, so values change continuously instead of only jumping at fixed breakpoints
A strict requirement that every single size value on the page must be expressed only in percentages, never in pixels
Automatic, built-in support for switching a page between a light color theme and a dark color theme based on OS setting
items.explanation: Fluid layout uses relative, formula-driven values (like clamp() with vw units) so a size can change smoothly across the whole range of widths, rather than staying constant until it jumps at a breakpoint.
items.reference:
Breakpoint: value jumps at fixed widths. Fluid: value changes continuously with viewport width.

Why: fluid layout is for continuous scale (type size, spacing), breakpoints are for discrete structure (column count).

items.prompt: A heading is 24px at every width below 900px, then instantly jumps to 40px at 900px and stays there. Is this fluid sizing?
choices: Yes, because the heading's rendered size does technically change at some point as the viewport keeps growing wider
No — a fluid value changes continuously across widths; this is a single breakpoint jump, the opposite pattern
Yes, since fluid sizing in this framing really just means 'the value isn't the exact same fixed number everywhere'
It genuinely depends entirely on which specific font family happens to be applied to that particular heading element
items.explanation: A single jump at one width is exactly what a breakpoint produces, not fluid sizing. Fluid sizing (e.g. via clamp() with vw units) changes the value smoothly across the range instead of holding it constant and then jumping.
items.reference:
Breakpoint: value jumps at fixed widths. Fluid: value changes continuously with viewport width.

Why: fluid layout is for continuous scale (type size, spacing), breakpoints are for discrete structure (column count).

items.prompt: Which of these is a better candidate for fluid sizing rather than a breakpoint jump?
choices: The number of grid columns rendered in a typical e-commerce product listing page across different screen widths
Whether a page's sidebar is currently shown fully expanded or instead collapsed down into a compact hamburger menu
A heading's font size scaling smoothly between a phone and a desktop
Whether a page's top navigation bar renders as a full horizontal row of links or instead as a compact hamburger menu
items.explanation: Column count, sidebar visibility, and nav style are all genuinely discrete states (a sidebar is either visible or it isn't) — breakpoint territory. Font size can sensibly take any value in a continuous range, which is what fluid sizing is for.
items.reference:
Breakpoint: value jumps at fixed widths. Fluid: value changes continuously with viewport width.

Why: fluid layout is for continuous scale (type size, spacing), breakpoints are for discrete structure (column count).

items.prompt: Per L1's comparison table, what's a key cost difference between responsive and adaptive design?
choices: Responsive design is, in every single case, always strictly cheaper to build and maintain than adaptive, with no exceptions
Adaptive means designing and maintaining several fixed layouts separately, while responsive designs once with more CSS complexity
There's genuinely no meaningful cost difference at all between choosing a responsive approach and choosing an adaptive one
Adaptive design, as an approach, requires writing and maintaining essentially no CSS at all across its various layouts
items.explanation: Responsive design is authored once but with more complex, flexible CSS to handle the full range of widths. Adaptive design means each fixed layout is its own design/maintenance surface — often 3-6 of them.
items.reference:
ResponsiveAdaptive
LayoutsOne, flexibleSeveral, fixed
Decided byBrowser, continuouslyClosest device match

items.prompt: A brand-new foldable device ships with a viewport width nobody had designed for. What happens under each strategy?
choices: Both strategies end up failing in exactly the identical way once a brand-new, previously unseen viewport width shows up
Responsive reflows automatically since it's continuous; adaptive needs a new fixed layout or falls back awkwardly to the nearest match
Adaptive design reflows automatically to handle it; responsive design instead needs an entirely new fixed layout built
Neither strategy, responsive or adaptive, is technically capable of ever handling a genuinely new device viewport width
items.explanation: Because responsive layouts compute continuously from actual width, a new width is just another point on the same continuum. Adaptive design has no in-between state — a new width either falls back to the nearest existing fixed layout or needs a new one built.
items.reference:
ResponsiveAdaptive
LayoutsOne, flexibleSeveral, fixed
Decided byBrowser, continuouslyClosest device match

items.prompt: Per L1, which is the more common default for modern websites?
choices: Adaptive design, always, across essentially every kind of modern website being built today regardless of its purpose
Responsive design, reaching for adaptive only for a handful of very different experiences
Neither responsive nor adaptive design is actually used much anymore in modern front-end web development practice
The choice between the two approaches is basically decided by a coin flip at the very start of each new project
items.explanation: Most production sites today are responsive-first. Adaptive is reserved for cases where the experience itself should genuinely differ per context, not just the layout size.
items.reference: Modern default: responsive. Adaptive: reserved for print layouts, kiosk modes, email clients with poor CSS support.

items.prompt: Which of these is the classic example of when adaptive design is still commonly chosen over responsive?
choices: A fairly typical marketing landing page built for a product launch, with no unusual platform or rendering constraints
An email template, because many email clients have poor or no support for modern CSS features
A personal blog site that only ever needs to render a single, fairly simple article layout template for its readers
A personal portfolio site built by an individual designer to showcase a small handful of their own past projects
items.explanation: Email clients frequently lack support for @media, @container, or clamp(), so email templates commonly ship as a small set of fixed, table-based layouts — a textbook adaptive case driven by platform constraints.
items.reference: Modern default: responsive. Adaptive: reserved for print layouts, kiosk modes, email clients with poor CSS support.

items.prompt: A team building a public kiosk/point-of-sale screen wants a deliberately different interaction model (larger touch targets, different information density) than their phone app, not just a resized version of it. What does L1/L3 suggest this points toward?
choices: This is actually exactly the kind of scenario that plain responsive design, with no adaptive layer, is well suited for
This is a case where the experience itself should differ, not just the layout — closer to adaptive design's use case
This particular problem should instead simply be solved by adding a larger number of additional breakpoints to the page
This particular problem is, in this framing, only genuinely solvable through the use of fluid typography techniques
items.explanation: When the interaction model and information density should genuinely differ per context — not just get resized — that's the adaptive case: a deliberately different, fixed experience for that context rather than one design reflowing.
items.reference: Modern default: responsive. Adaptive: reserved for print layouts, kiosk modes, email clients with poor CSS support.

items.prompt: Per L2, where should a breakpoint actually go?
choices: At a fixed set of standard device widths like exactly 375px and 768px, regardless of what this specific design actually needs
Wherever this specific design's own content starts to visibly strain, regardless of any device's width
At the precise pixel location that sits exactly halfway between the narrowest and widest viewport the team supports
Wherever the individual designer's own personal monitor happens to currently be sized at while they're working on it
items.explanation: A content-based breakpoint is chosen by resizing the actual layout until it visibly strains and putting the breakpoint there — which rarely lines up with a specific device's reported width and stays correct as new device sizes appear.
items.reference:
Device-based breakpoints: match a device chart, risk breaking at the wrong point. Content-based: resize until it strains, put the breakpoint there.

Why: a breakpoint should serve this design's content, not a device category.

items.prompt: A team sets a breakpoint at 768px because it's 'the tablet width,' but their three-column layout actually crushes its columns at 820px on a real tablet in landscape. What went wrong?
choices: Nothing at all went wrong here — a breakpoint set at exactly 768px is always considered correct for tablet devices
The breakpoint was chosen from a device chart instead of from where this specific content actually strains
The real underlying problem is that the layout itself simply needs more columns added, not a different breakpoint value
Tablet devices, as a category, don't actually support CSS breakpoints or media queries at all in their default browsers
items.explanation: 768px matched a device category, not this layout's actual content. The right breakpoint is found by resizing until the specific design strains, not by trusting a device-width chart, which is why it landed 52px off.
items.reference:
Device-based breakpoints: match a device chart, risk breaking at the wrong point. Content-based: resize until it strains, put the breakpoint there.

Why: a breakpoint should serve this design's content, not a device category.

items.prompt: Why is picking breakpoints from a device-width chart considered risky, per L2?
choices: Device-width charts like these are, as a category, always considered fundamentally inaccurate and unreliable to use
New devices with different widths keep appearing, and a device's reported width isn't guaranteed to match what CSS measures once browser chrome or zoom is involved
Physical devices, as a category, don't actually have consistent or stable reported widths across different models
It's genuinely not risky at all here — using a device-width chart is in fact the officially recommended approach to use
items.explanation: A device list is a moving target, and even a known device's CSS-measured width can differ from its marketing spec once browser chrome, zoom, or split-screen multitasking are factored in. Content-based breakpoints avoid depending on either.
items.reference:
Device-based breakpoints: match a device chart, risk breaking at the wrong point. Content-based: resize until it strains, put the breakpoint there.

Why: a breakpoint should serve this design's content, not a device category.

items.prompt: In mobile-first CSS, what do base (no media query) styles target, and what do breakpoints do?
choices: Base styles are written to target the widest possible screen size; breakpoints then progressively remove features
Base styles target the narrowest case; each breakpoint adds capability as more space becomes available
Base styles are written to target one specific, named device model; breakpoints end up being entirely unrelated to width
There's genuinely no meaningful practical difference at all here compared to the older, traditional desktop-first approach
items.explanation: Mobile-first means the unqualified base rules are written for the narrowest case, and min-width breakpoints layer on additional capability as space increases — an additive cascade.
items.reference:
Mobile-first (min-width): base = narrow, breakpoints add. Desktop-first (max-width): base = wide, breakpoints subtract.

Why: additive overrides are easier to reason about as more breakpoints get added over time.

items.prompt: Which media query syntax is characteristic of a mobile-first approach?
choices: @media (max-width: ...) used exclusively throughout the whole stylesheet, with no min-width queries present anywhere
@media (min-width: ...), layering rules on as the viewport grows
@media (device-type: mobile), a hypothetical syntax that directly targets a device's reported category rather than its width
No media queries of any kind at all, relying purely on flexible units and layout techniques without any breakpoints
items.explanation: min-width queries only apply once the viewport reaches or exceeds that width, matching mobile-first's additive, 'add capability as space appears' model.
items.reference:
Mobile-first (min-width): base = narrow, breakpoints add. Desktop-first (max-width): base = wide, breakpoints subtract.

Why: additive overrides are easier to reason about as more breakpoints get added over time.

items.prompt: Per L2, why is mobile-first the dominant convention today, beyond mobile traffic being the majority case?
choices: Because max-width media queries, as a technique, simply don't function correctly in the vast majority of modern browsers
Because it keeps overrides additive (turning features on) rather than subtractive (turning them off), which stays easier to reason about as more breakpoints accumulate
Because writing styles the mobile-first way requires noticeably less total CSS overall compared to desktop-first, in every case
Because the older desktop-first approach is, as a technique, now considered formally deprecated and no longer supported
items.explanation: Additive cascades (mobile-first) stay easier to reason about as a page grows more breakpoints, since each new rule only adds capability. Subtractive cascades (desktop-first) require every narrower rule to correctly undo wide-screen assumptions.
items.reference:
Mobile-first (min-width): base = narrow, breakpoints add. Desktop-first (max-width): base = wide, breakpoints subtract.

Why: additive overrides are easier to reason about as more breakpoints get added over time.

items.prompt: What do the three arguments of CSS clamp(min, preferred, max) mean?
choices: Three entirely separate color values that the browser is expected to choose between depending on the current theme
A floor value, a formula (often using vw) that scales with viewport, and a ceiling value
Three fixed pixel values representing three separate, hardcoded breakpoints the layout is expected to snap between
The minimum, average, and maximum permitted number of grid columns the layout is allowed to render at any given width
items.explanation: clamp() picks the 'preferred' middle value unless it would fall below min or above max, in which case it's clamped to that bound. The preferred term is typically a formula using vw units so it scales continuously with viewport width.
items.reference:
font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 1rem + 3vw, 3rem); — never below 1.5rem, never above 3rem, scales in between.

Why: clamp() replaces a breakpoint jump with a continuous formula between a floor and a ceiling.

items.prompt: font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 1rem + 3vw, 3rem) is applied. At a very narrow viewport where '1rem + 3vw' evaluates to 1.2rem, what font size is actually used?
choices: 1.2rem, exactly as computed by the formula, with no adjustment applied regardless of the stated floor and ceiling
1.5rem — the formula's result is below the floor, so it clamps to the minimum
3rem, the stated maximum value, applied here regardless of what the formula itself actually computes at this width
0rem, meaning the text effectively disappears entirely from the rendered page at this particular narrow viewport width
items.explanation: clamp() never lets the preferred value go below the minimum bound. Since 1.2rem is under the 1.5rem floor, the actual rendered size clamps up to 1.5rem.
items.reference:
font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 1rem + 3vw, 3rem); — never below 1.5rem, never above 3rem, scales in between.

Why: clamp() replaces a breakpoint jump with a continuous formula between a floor and a ceiling.

items.prompt: Why does the 'preferred' term of a clamp() formula typically include a vw unit rather than being a fixed rem value?
choices: Because the CSS specification itself technically requires that a vw unit always be present somewhere inside clamp()
Because vw is a percentage of viewport width, so the formula's output changes continuously as the viewport resizes, instead of staying constant
Because values expressed in vw units are known to render measurably faster in the browser than equivalent rem values
There's genuinely no real underlying reason for this at all, it's simply an arbitrary convention authors tend to follow
items.explanation: 1vw equals 1% of viewport width, so a formula like '1rem + 3vw' produces a different value at every viewport width. A fixed rem value wouldn't change at all, defeating the point of fluid sizing.
items.reference:
font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 1rem + 3vw, 3rem); — never below 1.5rem, never above 3rem, scales in between.

Why: clamp() replaces a breakpoint jump with a continuous formula between a floor and a ceiling.

items.prompt: Per L2, when should a value use a breakpoint instead of fluid clamp() sizing?
choices: Never under any circumstance — clamp() is intended to fully and completely replace every breakpoint in modern CSS
When the value is genuinely discrete, like a grid's column count, which can't sensibly be '2.4 columns'
Only in the specific, narrow case where the value being styled happens to be a color rather than a size or spacing
Only in the specific, narrow case where the layout is currently being viewed on a mobile-sized viewport specifically
items.explanation: Breakpoints suit genuinely discrete states — a grid has 1, 2, or 4 columns, never a fractional in-between value. Fluid sizing suits values that can meaningfully take any number in a range, like font size.
items.reference:
Breakpoint-onlyFluid (clamp)
Between breakpointsConstant, jumpsChanges continuously
Best forStructureContinuous scale

items.prompt: A real production page typically uses both breakpoints and fluid clamp() values together. Why isn't one enough on its own?
choices: Using both breakpoints and clamp() together on the same page is considered redundant and should generally be avoided
Because a page usually has both discrete structural decisions (column count, nav style) and continuous scale decisions (font size, spacing) that call for different tools
Because clamp(), as a CSS function, technically cannot function correctly without at least one breakpoint also present
Because breakpoints, as a technique, are in the process of being fully deprecated in modern CSS in favor of clamp() alone
items.explanation: Structural changes (like column count) are discrete and suit breakpoints; scale changes (like font size) are continuous and suit clamp(). Most real pages have both kinds of decisions, so both tools are used together, not as substitutes.
items.reference:
Breakpoint-onlyFluid (clamp)
Between breakpointsConstant, jumpsChanges continuously
Best forStructureContinuous scale

items.prompt: What's the practical difference between writing a rule inside @media (min-width: 768px) versus @media (max-width: 768px)?
choices: They're functionally identical here — min-width and max-width are really just two alternate spellings of the same query
min-width applies the rule once the viewport reaches or exceeds 768px; max-width applies it while the viewport is at or below 768px — opposite directions
min-width queries only ever apply correctly on mobile devices specifically; max-width queries only apply on desktop
max-width, as a media feature, is formally deprecated and is therefore no longer supported in any current browser
items.explanation: min-width is a floor — the rule activates at that width and above, which is why it pairs with mobile-first's additive model. max-width is a ceiling — the rule activates at that width and below, pairing with desktop-first's subtractive model.
items.reference:
min-width: 768px → applies at 768px and above. max-width: 768px → applies at 768px and below.

Why: the two point in opposite directions, which is what makes mobile-first vs. desktop-first genuinely different cascades, not just different syntax.

items.prompt: A stylesheet mixes @media (min-width: 640px) rules and @media (max-width: 900px) rules for the same element, in the same project. What's the risk?
choices: There's genuinely no risk at all here — mixing min-width and max-width rules together is always considered perfectly safe
Between 640px and 900px, both rule sets can be active at once, and source order (not clear intent) decides which wins — harder to reason about than committing to one direction
The browser will, in this specific case, simply refuse outright to apply either one of the two conflicting rule sets
Mixing the two query directions like this automatically and silently triggers a fallback to full adaptive design instead
items.explanation: Mixing min-width and max-width breakpoints for the same element means their ranges can overlap, and which rule ultimately applies depends on CSS source order rather than a clear 'narrow vs. wide' intent — this is exactly why picking one direction (mobile-first, in most modern projects) and staying consistent matters.
items.reference:
min-width: 768px → applies at 768px and above. max-width: 768px → applies at 768px and below.

Why: the two point in opposite directions, which is what makes mobile-first vs. desktop-first genuinely different cascades, not just different syntax.

items.prompt: Why can't a @media breakpoint alone handle a product card that needs to switch to a vertical layout only when a sidebar opens and eats its horizontal space?
choices: @media queries, as a CSS feature, are technically only allowed to be used a single time within any one given stylesheet
@media only measures the viewport, never the width of the specific element being styled — so it can't tell a wide-viewport/narrow-card case from a wide-viewport/wide-card case
Product cards, as a type of component, can genuinely never be styled using @media queries under any circumstance at all
@media queries, as implemented in modern browsers, simply don't support being combined with flexbox-based layouts at all
items.explanation: A card that's 220px wide because a sidebar opened, and a card that's 220px wide on a narrow phone viewport, look identical to @media — both only see the viewport width, not the card's actual box width.
items.reference:
@container card (min-width: 360px) { ... } — reacts to the card's own box, not the viewport.

Why: container queries fix the case where a component's context (not the viewport) changes its available width.

items.prompt: What does a CSS container query (@container) measure, that a media query (@media) does not?
choices: The specific operating system currently running on the visitor's device, as reported through a dedicated CSS media feature
The width of a specific named containing element's box, rather than the browser viewport
The total number of distinct colors currently present and rendered anywhere at all on the given page being styled
Only the device's screen pixel density value, with no actual information at all about any element's rendered width
items.explanation: container-type: inline-size marks an element as a query container; @container then measures that specific box's width, which can shrink or grow independently of the viewport (e.g. when a sidebar opens).
items.reference:
@container card (min-width: 360px) { ... } — reacts to the card's own box, not the viewport.

Why: container queries fix the case where a component's context (not the viewport) changes its available width.

items.prompt: A card component is reused in a sidebar-adjacent grid, a full-width 'related products' row, and a narrow modal — all on the exact same page viewport. Which query type correctly lets the card adapt to each placement?
choices: @media, since in this particular scenario it's ultimately the overall page viewport width that genuinely matters most
@container, since it's the card's own box width that differs across placements, not the viewport
Neither @media nor @container can handle this case at all — it would genuinely require custom JavaScript to solve
@page, a CSS at-rule intended specifically for controlling how printed pages are formatted, not for adapting live card layouts
items.explanation: Since the viewport doesn't change across these three placements but the card's own available width does, only a container query (measuring the card's box) can distinguish between them — a media query would see identical conditions in all three.
items.reference:
@container card (min-width: 360px) { ... } — reacts to the card's own box, not the viewport.

Why: container queries fix the case where a component's context (not the viewport) changes its available width.

items.prompt: A heading should be 32px at a 500px viewport and 56px at a 1300px viewport. Following L3's worked recipe, what's the slope (change in px per 1px of viewport width)?
choices: (56 + 32) / (1300 + 500) = 88 / 1800, which comes out to roughly 0.048px of font size per 1px of viewport width
56 / 1300, which comes out to roughly 0.043px of font size change for every single 1px increase in viewport width
There's genuinely no reliable way to compute this slope value at all without opening up a dedicated design tool first
items.explanation: Slope is (target max - target min) / (viewport max - viewport min) = (56 - 32) / (1300 - 500) = 24 / 800 = 0.03px of font size per 1px of viewport width, which becomes 3vw in the formula (0.03 * 100).
items.reference:
Recipe: slope = (max - min) / (vwMax - vwMin); intercept = min - slope * vwMin; result: clamp(min, intercept + slope*100 + 'vw', max).

Why: this turns 'A at width W1, B at width W2' into an exact clamp() line.

items.prompt: Using the same target (32px at 500px viewport, 56px at 1300px viewport, slope 0.03px/px = 3vw), what is the intercept term (the value the formula predicts at 0vw)?
choices: 32 minus 0.03 times 500, which works out to 32 minus 15, giving an intercept value of exactly 17px at zero viewport width
56 minus 0.03 times 1300, which works out to exactly 17px as well, arrived at independently through the other known point
Both A and B are correct — either point on the line gives the same intercept
0px exactly, since every clamp() formula of this kind is defined to always start its calculation from a zero baseline
items.explanation: The intercept is where the line would cross 0vw, and since it's the same line, computing it from either known point gives the same answer: 32 - 0.03*500 = 17, and 56 - 0.03*1300 = 17. Both calculations confirming each other is exactly how you'd sanity-check the formula.
items.reference:
Recipe: slope = (max - min) / (vwMax - vwMin); intercept = min - slope * vwMin; result: clamp(min, intercept + slope*100 + 'vw', max).

Why: this turns 'A at width W1, B at width W2' into an exact clamp() line.

items.prompt: A clamp() recipe is applied where the minimum and maximum are set to the exact same value (e.g. clamp(15px, 15px, 15px)). What happens?
choices: The resulting value ends up oscillating unpredictably back and forth between the floor and ceiling as the viewport resizes
The value is fixed at that number at every viewport width — the slope becomes irrelevant since it can never legally exceed a floor and ceiling that are identical
Writing a clamp() with an identical floor and ceiling like this one causes a hard CSS parse error in every modern browser
It behaves exactly like an ordinary, genuinely fluid clamp() with clearly visible smooth scaling across the full viewport range
items.explanation: When min equals max, the result is clamped to that single value everywhere. A fixed value would produce the identical result with less to read — reaching for clamp() here adds unneeded complexity rather than solving a real scaling need.
items.reference:
Recipe: slope = (max - min) / (vwMax - vwMin); intercept = min - slope * vwMin; result: clamp(min, intercept + slope*100 + 'vw', max).

Why: this turns 'A at width W1, B at width W2' into an exact clamp() line.

items.prompt: A responsive grid keeps adding/stretching columns as the viewport grows, with no upper limit. What happens on a 3840px 4K monitor, and what fixes it?
choices: Nothing at all happens in this case — responsive design, by its very nature, has no meaningful upper-limit problem to worry about
Content stretches uncomfortably wide (e.g. product photos scaled comically large); a max-width on the wrapping container plus centering fixes it
The browser automatically and silently caps the rendered content's width at exactly 1920px with no author CSS needed
This particular problem can genuinely only ever be fixed by abandoning responsive design entirely in favor of adaptive
items.explanation: Without a cap, a responsive layout keeps filling available width indefinitely, which reads as stretched-thin on very wide screens. A max-width on the wrapper plus margin-inline: auto centers the content and stops it from over-stretching, while still remaining a single responsive layout.
items.reference:
.listing-wrap { max-width: 1600px; margin-inline: auto; }

Why: 'responsive' should mean 'adapts within a sensible range,' not 'always fills 100% of any width.'

items.prompt: Why is an unbounded-stretch bug (missing max-width) easy to miss during typical testing?
choices: It's actually quite easy to catch and reproduce this specific bug on literally any ordinary laptop-sized screen or display
It only shows up at very wide viewports (ultra-wide/4K), which a normal laptop-width test pass doesn't cover
This particular bug, by its nature, is one that genuinely only ever affects mobile devices and their narrower viewports
This is fundamentally a server-side rendering bug in this case, rather than something caused by the page's own CSS rules
items.explanation: Testing only up to a typical laptop width (say 1440px) never triggers this bug — it only appears once the viewport is wide enough that the grid runs out of columns to add and starts stretching existing content instead.
items.reference:
.listing-wrap { max-width: 1600px; margin-inline: auto; }

Why: 'responsive' should mean 'adapts within a sensible range,' not 'always fills 100% of any width.'

items.prompt: What does WCAG 1.4.10 (Reflow) actually require?
choices: That every single page on a site must formally support a minimum of at least three distinct, separately defined breakpoints
That content remain usable without horizontal scrolling when zoomed to 400%, on a viewport equivalent to 320px CSS pixels wide
That all body text across an entire site must use a minimum font size of exactly 16px, with no smaller text permitted anywhere
That every page on a site must fully load and become interactive to the visitor in under three seconds total, every time
items.explanation: 1.4.10 is a specific, testable requirement: at 400% zoom on an effective 320px-wide viewport, content must reflow to remain usable without needing to scroll horizontally (with limited exceptions like data tables).
items.reference:
WCAG 1.4.10: no horizontal scroll needed at 400% zoom on a 320px-equivalent viewport.

Why: a layout that looks fine at 100% zoom can still fail this real, testable accessibility floor.

items.prompt: A page looks perfect at 100% zoom on every device tested. Why might it still fail an accessibility check?
choices: It genuinely can't fail in that case — testing at 100% zoom across a representative range of devices is already fully sufficient
Because reflow requirements (WCAG 1.4.10) test zoomed-in width (400% zoom on a 320px-equivalent viewport), which is a different, narrower effective width than any physical device test covers
Because formal accessibility checks of this kind are, in general, only ever really concerned with color contrast ratios specifically
Because the zoom level a page is viewed at genuinely has no real, meaningful relationship at all to its effective layout width
items.explanation: Zooming to 400% effectively shrinks the usable viewport width dramatically — testing only physical device widths at 100% zoom never exercises this narrower effective width, which is exactly where a clamp() floor set too high can still fail.
items.reference:
WCAG 1.4.10: no horizontal scroll needed at 400% zoom on a 320px-equivalent viewport.

Why: a layout that looks fine at 100% zoom can still fail this real, testable accessibility floor.

items.prompt: Per L3, what's the deeper signal that a case genuinely calls for adaptive design rather than 'just add more breakpoints' to a responsive page?
choices: The page in question already happens to have more than three separate breakpoints defined somewhere in its stylesheet
The content and interaction model should genuinely differ per context (not just resize), e.g. a warehouse tablet needing larger tap targets and fewer decorative images than a consumer phone app
The page in question happens to use the CSS clamp() function anywhere at all within its existing set of style rules
The team working on the project simply happens to personally prefer writing out several separate templates by hand
items.explanation: More breakpoints only helps when it's still the same design reflowing. When the actual content, density, or interaction model needs to differ by context — not just get resized — that's a sign the honest answer is a separate, adaptive template, not another breakpoint.
items.reference:
Adaptive still wins for: email clients (CSS support), kiosk/POS (different interaction model), print (content stripped, not reflowed).

Why: the judgment call is recognizing when it's no longer the same design at all.

items.prompt: Why is a dedicated print stylesheet (@media print) described as 'adaptive in spirit, even though implemented with the responsive toolset'?
choices: Because dedicated print stylesheets, as a CSS feature, technically don't make any use of actual CSS rules at all
Because the print layout typically strips navigation and interactive elements entirely rather than reflowing them, which is closer to a discrete experience swap than a continuous reflow
Because using @media print, as a technique, technically requires maintaining an entirely separate standalone HTML file
Because print stylesheets, as implemented in modern browsers, are technically incapable of making use of breakpoints at all
items.explanation: Even though @media is the responsive mechanism, a print stylesheet's actual behavior — removing interactive chrome outright rather than reflowing it — matches adaptive design's spirit: a deliberately different, fixed experience for that context.
items.reference:
Adaptive still wins for: email clients (CSS support), kiosk/POS (different interaction model), print (content stripped, not reflowed).

Why: the judgment call is recognizing when it's no longer the same design at all.

items.prompt: Testing a layout at exactly 375px, 768px, and 1440px (three fixed presets) missed a bug that only appears at 820px. What testing practice would have caught it?
choices: Testing the layout at an even larger number of additional fixed presets, for example adding both 400px and 900px to the list
Dragging the browser width continuously rather than only checking fixed preset widths
Relying exclusively on testing the layout on a small set of real physical devices pulled from a drawer in the office
Switching the entire project over to adaptive design instead, specifically so that fixed presets are no longer needed at all
items.explanation: Any finite set of fixed presets can straddle a real problem width. Continuously dragging the viewport width exposes the exact pixel range where a breakpoint is set wrong, which spot-checking fixed presets can miss entirely.

items.prompt: Why does testing a reusable card component only at the page's narrowest and widest viewport miss real bugs, per L3?
choices: It genuinely doesn't miss anything meaningful here — testing only at the page's two viewport extremes is already fully sufficient for every component

Because a container-query-driven component's layout depends on its own container's width, which can differ from the page viewport (e.g. sidebar open vs. closed) — testing only viewport extremes skips those in-between container widths
Because individual components, by their very nature, can genuinely never be meaningfully tested independently of the entire surrounding page
Because card components, as a category of UI element, essentially never make any real practical use of container queries at all
items.explanation: A component's actual rendered width can vary with its container context, independent of the page viewport. Testing only page-viewport extremes can entirely skip the specific container widths where a @container breakpoint bug would show up.
